name: Inca Empire
summary: Tawantinsuyu, the largest empire in pre-Columbian America, linked by a vast road network and run without a written script using knotted-cord records (khipu).

location.value: Along the Andes: Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, much of Chile, northwest Argentina and southwest Colombia. Capital Cusco.

terrain.value: High mountains, coastal desert and valleys, linked by the 40,000 km road network (Qhapaq Ñan).

climate.value: From cold highlands to arid coast. Farming was terraced and irrigated.

resources.value: Potatoes, maize, quinoa, llamas and alpacas, cotton, gold and silver.

disasters.value: Smallpox reached the Andes before the Spanish, in the 1520s, killing the emperor Huayna Capac and his heir.

population.value: About 12 million in the early 16th century (Wikipedia infobox). Estimates range widely, from 4 to 37 million.

urbanisation.value: Cusco was the capital. Machu Picchu was a royal estate.

disease.value: Repeated epidemics after contact (smallpox, typhus, influenza, measles).

migration.value: The mitma system forcibly resettled communities to secure conquered lands.

economicBase.value: An economy that worked largely without money or markets, based on reciprocity and labour tax (mitʼa) on state and religious lands.

tradeRoutes.value: The road network and storehouses (qullqas) moved goods. There was little private trade.

moneyAndTax.value: No money. Taxes were paid in labour (mitʼa).

inequality.value: The Sapa Inca and a small noble class ruled millions of subjects.

governmentType.value: A divine, absolute monarchy: the Sapa Inca was “son of the Sun”. Four quarters (suyus) under governors.

keyRulers.value: Pachacuti (1438–1471, founder of the empire). Topa Inca Yupanqui (1471–1493). Huayna Capac (1493–1525). Huáscar and Atahualpa (civil war). Túpac Amaru (last Neo-Inca ruler, executed 1572).

succession.value: Hereditary, but disputed: the civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa (1529–1532).

institutions.value: The mitʼa labour system, state storehouses, road relay stations (tambos), and quipu record-keeping.

stability.value: The civil war (1529–1532) weakened the empire just before the Spanish arrived.

eliteConflict.value: Rival royal lineages backing different heirs.

armyAndTech.value: Large armies of conscripted soldiers with slings, clubs and spears, and fortresses (Sacsayhuamán). No iron or horses.

majorWars.value: The Chanka war (Pachacuti’s rise), the conquest of Chimor, and the Spanish conquest (Cajamarca 1532, Atahualpa executed 1533).

territoryChange.value: About 2 million km² in 1527 (Wikipedia infobox), the largest empire in pre-Columbian America.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Chanka, Chimor, Amazon peoples and the Mapuche.

inventions.value: Mortarless fitted stonework, the Qhapaq Ñan road system, suspension bridges, terracing, and quipu knotted-string records.

scienceEducation.value: Quipus recorded numbers in base 10 (whether they also recorded narratives is debated). Skilled trepanation surgery.

openness.value: Absorbed conquered peoples’ gods and skills.

religion.value: Inca religion centred on the Sun god Inti, with the emperor as his son, plus local huacas (sacred places).

languageWriting.value: Quechua (official), Aymara and others. Records were kept on quipus, not writing.

artsArchitecture.value: Machu Picchu, Sacsayhuamán, the Coricancha temple, and fine textiles.

socialStructure.value: Sapa Inca, Inca nobles, local lords (kurakas) and commoners organised in ayllus (kin groups).

sharedIdentity.value: Tawantinsuyu, the “Realm of the Four Parts”, united by Quechua and the Sun cult.

neighbours.value: Chimor, Amazonian peoples and the Mapuche, then the Spanish.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Quechua across the Andes, where it is still spoken by millions.

colonisation.value: A conquering empire that resettled peoples. It was itself conquered by Spain from 1532 (Neo-Inca state to 1572).

riseSignals.value: Pachacuti’s victory over the Chanka (1438), then rapid conquest, efficient roads and storehouses.

declineSignals.value: The smallpox epidemic of the 1520s, the civil war of 1529–1532, and the Spanish invasion.

outcome.value: Conquest. Pizarro captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca (1532) and executed him (1533). The last Neo-Inca stronghold at Vilcabamba fell in 1572.

sources.value: Spanish chroniclers (Cieza de León, Garcilaso de la Vega, Guaman Poma), quipus (not fully read) and archaeology. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also D’Altroy (2014).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Population figures vary hugely and the early chronology is uncertain. The end is dated 1533 or 1572.
